topics.title: Sounds: ai, ay, ee, ea, igh
topics.intro: The same sound can be spelt in different ways. “ai” in rain and “ay” in play make the same sound. Let’s spot them!
topics.teach: Explain two different ways to spell the sound in “rain”.
topics.talk: Ask {him} to find three words with “ay” on a cereal box or in a book.

topics.title: Sounds: oa, ow, oo, ar, or, ir, ou, oi, air
topics.intro: More sounds with more than one spelling: snow and boat, moon and blue, bird and turn.
topics.teach: Explain why “ow” can be tricky (cow or snow?).
topics.talk: Play “I spy” with sounds: I spy something with an “oo” sound.

topics.title: Tricky letters: ph, wh, soft c and g, silent letters
topics.intro: Some letters play tricks: ph says “f”, the k in knight is silent, and c says “s” in city.
topics.teach: Explain what a silent letter is, with an example.
topics.talk: Find a silent letter in a word on a sign.

topics.title: Wonderful words
topics.intro: Great readers and writers use exciting words. Instead of “big”, why not “enormous” or “gigantic”?
topics.teach: Use three of today’s words in a sentence about your favourite superhero.
topics.talk: Ask {him} to describe dinner using one of the wonderful words.

topics.title: Fables: stories with a lesson
topics.intro: Fables are very old stories, often about animals, that teach a lesson called a moral. Read each one carefully, then answer the questions.
topics.teach: Explain what the moral of “The Hare and the Tortoise” is.
topics.talk: Ask {him} which fable {she} liked best and what lesson it teaches.

topics.title: Adventure stories: racing, space and heroes
topics.intro: Three adventure stories. Read each one, then answer questions about what happens, how characters feel, and why.
topics.teach: Explain how Turbo felt at the start of the race and at the end.
topics.talk: Ask {him} who the real hero was in “The Quiet Hero” and why.

topics.title: Fact files
topics.intro: Non-fiction gives us facts. Look for headings, numbers and key words to find answers fast.
topics.teach: Explain one difference between a story and a fact file.
topics.talk: Ask {him} for three facts about racing cars.

topics.title: Peter Rabbit
topics.intro: The Tale of Peter Rabbit was written by Beatrix Potter more than 120 years ago. Some words are old-fashioned, so read slowly and use clues.
topics.teach: Explain why Peter got into trouble.
topics.talk: Read the story together and ask {him} to predict what happens next.

topics.title: Poems: trains, shadows and windy nights
topics.intro: Poems use rhythm and rhyme to make pictures in your head. Read these aloud: you can hear the train rattling!
topics.teach: Explain how the train poem sounds like a train.
topics.talk: Read “From a Railway Carriage” aloud together, faster and faster.

items.prompt: Which word has the same sound as the “ai” in rain?
items.explain: “ay” in play makes the same sound as “ai” in rain.

items.prompt: Which word has the same sound as the “ay” in day?
items.explain: a-e (a, a letter, e) in cake makes the same sound: split digraph.

items.prompt: Which spelling is right?
items.explain: “ai” usually comes in the middle of a word: train, rain, paint.

items.prompt: Which spelling is right?
items.explain: “ay” usually comes at the END of a word: day, play, today.

items.prompt: Which word has the same sound as the “ee” in tree?
items.explain: “ea” in beach makes the same sound as “ee”.

items.prompt: Which word has the same sound as the “ee” in see?
items.explain: e-e in these is a split digraph making the “ee” sound.

items.prompt: Which spelling is right?
items.explain: Most “ee” words in the middle use “ee” or “ea”: you have to learn which. sleep, feet, green.

items.prompt: Which word has the same sound as the “igh” in night?
items.explain: “ie” in pie makes the same sound as “igh”.

items.prompt: Which word has the same sound as the “i-e” in bike?
items.explain: A “y” at the end of a short word often says “igh”: fly, my, sky, cry.

items.prompt: Which spelling is right?
items.explain: “igh” is common: light, night, bright, fight.

items.prompt: Which word has the same sound as the “oa” in boat?
items.explain: “ow” can say “oa” (snow, slow) or “ow” (cow, now). Here it is snow.

items.prompt: Which word has the same sound as the “o-e” in home?
items.explain: “oa” in toast and “o-e” in home make the same sound.

items.prompt: Which word has the same sound as the “oo” in moon?
items.explain: “ue” in blue makes the long “oo” sound.

items.prompt: Which word has the same sound as the “ew” in new?
items.explain: u-e in tune makes the same sound as “ew”.

items.prompt: Which word has the same sound as the “ar” in car?
items.explain: “ar” as in car, star, start, park.

items.prompt: Which word has the same sound as the “or” in fork?
items.explain: “aw” in saw makes the same sound as “or”.

items.prompt: Which word has the same sound as the “ir” in bird?
items.explain: “ur” in turn and “ir” in bird make the same sound. So does “er” in her.

items.prompt: Which word has the same sound as the “ou” in cloud?
items.explain: “ow” in town makes the same sound as “ou” in cloud.

items.prompt: Which word has the same sound as the “oi” in coin?
items.explain: “oy” usually comes at the end (boy, toy); “oi” in the middle (coin, point).

items.prompt: Which word has the same sound as the “air” in hair?
items.explain: “ear” can say “air” (bear, wear) or “eer” (hear, ear).

items.prompt: In “phone”, what sound do the letters “ph” make?
items.explain: “ph” says “f”: phone, photo, dolphin, elephant.

items.prompt: Which word starts with the same sound as “when”?
items.explain: “wh” at the start of when, where, which sounds like “w”.

items.prompt: In “city”, what sound does the “c” make?
items.explain: Before e, i or y, c says “s”: city, ice, cycle. This is a soft c.

items.prompt: In “giant”, what sound does the “g” make?
items.explain: Before e, i or y, g often says “j”: giant, magic, energy. This is a soft g.

items.prompt: In “knight”, which letter is silent at the start?
items.explain: The k in kn- words is silent: knee, knock, knight, know.

items.prompt: In “write”, which letter is silent at the start?
items.explain: The w in wr- words is silent: write, wrong, wrap.

items.prompt: What sound do the letters “-tion” make at the end of “station”?
items.explain: -tion says “shun”: station, action, nation, motion.

items.prompt: Which word has the same “zh” sound as “treasure”?
items.explain: “-sure” in treasure and measure makes the “zh” sound.

items.prompt: Which spelling of the “j” sound is used at the end of “bridge”?
items.explain: After a short vowel, use -dge: bridge, badge, hedge. After other sounds, -ge: huge, large.

items.prompt: How do you make the plural of “baby”?
items.explain: If a word ends consonant + y, change the y to i and add -es.

items.prompt: Why did the hare stop during the race?
items.answer: he was so sure he would win that he had a nap
items.explain: “He was so sure he would win that he lay down under a tree for a nap.”
items.passage:
The Hare and the Tortoise

A hare was always boasting about how fast he could run. “Nobody can beat me,” he said.

The tortoise looked up slowly. “I will race you,” she said.

The hare laughed so hard he nearly fell over. But the race began. The hare dashed away and was soon far ahead. He was so sure he would win that he lay down under a tree for a nap.

The tortoise kept going, one slow step after another, never stopping.

When the hare woke up, he raced to the finish line. But the tortoise was already there, waiting.

Slow and steady wins the race.
items.passageSource: A fable by Aesop, retold for this app

items.prompt: What woke the lion up?
items.answer: a mouse ran across his nose
items.explain: “A tiny mouse ran across his nose.”
items.passage:
The Lion and the Mouse

A lion was sleeping in the sun when a tiny mouse ran across his nose. The lion woke up and caught the mouse in his huge paw.

“Please let me go,” squeaked the mouse. “One day I might help you.”

The lion laughed. How could a little mouse ever help a mighty lion? But he let her go.

A few days later, the lion was caught in a hunter’s net. He roared and roared, but he could not get free.

The mouse heard him. She ran to the net and nibbled through the ropes until the lion was free.

“You laughed at me,” said the mouse, “but even a little friend can be a great help.”
items.passageSource: A fable by Aesop, retold for this app

items.prompt: What did Blaze say to Turbo before the race?

options.feedback: Blaze was not kind at the start.
Look at what Blaze laughed.

items.explain: Blaze laughed: “You’re too small to win.”
items.passage:
The Big Race

The stadium lights blazed. Turbo, a small red racing car, rolled up to the starting line. Next to him was Blaze, the fastest car in the league, revving his engine loudly.

“You’re too small to win,” Blaze laughed.

Turbo said nothing. He had been practising the bendy corners every night.

The flag dropped! Blaze zoomed ahead on the long straight road. But when the track twisted like a snake, Blaze skidded wide. Turbo hugged the corners, smooth and steady.

On the last lap, Blaze’s tyres were worn out. Turbo crept past him, then pushed his engine as hard as it would go. He crossed the line first by the length of a bumper!

Blaze rolled over, smiling for the first time. “I was wrong,” he said. “It’s not about size. It’s about practice.”
items.passageSource: A story written for this app

items.prompt: Why did Bleep get lost?

options.text: He wandered off to look at something shiny

options.feedback: The wind howled, but he got lost by wandering off.

options.text: Captain Nova left him on purpose
options.feedback: She told him to stay close.

items.explain: “Bleep spotted something shiny behind a rock and wobbled off to look.”
items.passage:
The Lost Droid

Captain Nova’s spaceship landed on a frosty purple planet. Her little droid, Bleep, beeped nervously. Bleep did not like the cold.

“We need to find the crystal that powers our ship,” said Captain Nova. “Stay close.”

But Bleep spotted something shiny behind a rock and wobbled off to look. When he turned round, the captain had gone. The wind howled. Bleep’s lights flickered blue with fear.

Then Bleep remembered his training. He switched on his signal beam and pointed it at the sky. Far away, Captain Nova saw a bright stripe of light.

She ran towards it and found Bleep beside a glowing green crystal: the very one they needed!

“You got lost,” she said, “but you also found exactly what we were looking for.” Bleep beeped proudly all the way home.
items.passageSource: A story written for this app

items.passage:
The Lost Droid

Captain Nova’s spaceship landed on a frosty purple planet. Her little droid, Bleep, beeped nervously. Bleep did not like the cold.

“We need to find the crystal that powers our ship,” said Captain Nova. “Stay close.”

But Bleep spotted something shiny behind a rock and wobbled off to look. When he turned round, the captain had gone. The wind howled. Bleep’s lights flickered blue with fear.

Then Bleep remembered his training. He switched on his signal beam and pointed it at the sky. Far away, Captain Nova saw a bright stripe of light.

She ran towards it and found Bleep beside a glowing green crystal: the very one they needed!

“You got lost,” she said, “but you also found exactly what we were looking for.” Bleep beeped proudly all the way home.

items.passage:
The Quiet Hero

Everyone in Brickton knew about Thunderbolt. He could fly faster than a jet and lift a bus with one hand. But nobody knew about Pip.

Pip had no cape and no superpowers. She ran the little bakery on the corner.

One stormy evening, the power went out across the whole town. Thunderbolt zoomed off to fix the broken power station. Meanwhile, the streets grew dark and cold, and people were frightened.

Pip lit every candle in her bakery. She opened the doors and called, “Come in! It’s warm in here!” All night long she handed out hot bread and kind words.

In the morning, when the lights came back on, Thunderbolt landed outside the bakery. He saw the crowd of happy, sleepy people.

“You’re a hero too,” he told Pip. She just smiled and offered him a bun.

items.prompt: In which year did people first walk on the Moon?
items.explain: “On 20 July 1969.”
items.passage:
Fact file: Footprints on the Moon

On 20 July 1969, two American astronauts became the first people to walk on the Moon. Their names were Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin. A third astronaut, Michael Collins, stayed in the spacecraft circling above.

The journey to the Moon took about three days. The astronauts wore special spacesuits because there is no air to breathe on the Moon.

When Neil Armstrong stepped onto the dusty ground, he said, “That’s one small step for man, one giant leap for mankind.”

There is no wind on the Moon, so the astronauts’ footprints are probably still there today!

items.passage:
Fact file: Racing cars

Racing cars are built to go very fast. They are low to the ground and have a smooth, pointed shape so the air flows over them easily.

Racing tyres are wide and have no grooves when the track is dry. This helps them grip the road. In the rain, drivers change to tyres with grooves to push the water away.

During a race, cars drive into the pit lane for a pit stop. A team of mechanics can change all four tyres in about two seconds!

Drivers wear a fireproof suit and a strong helmet to keep them safe. Some races are more than 300 kilometres long, so drivers must be very fit.

items.passage:
Once upon a time there were four little Rabbits, and their names were—

Flopsy, Mopsy, Cotton-tail, and Peter.

They lived with their Mother in a sand-bank, underneath the root of a very big fir-tree.

‘Now my dears,’ said old Mrs. Rabbit one morning, ‘you may go into the fields or down the lane, but don’t go into Mr. McGregor’s garden: your Father had an accident there; he was put in a pie by Mrs. McGregor.’

‘Now run along, and don’t get into mischief. I am going out.’

Then old Mrs. Rabbit took a basket and her umbrella, and went through the wood to the baker’s. She bought a loaf of brown bread and five currant buns.

Flopsy, Mopsy, and Cottontail, who were good little bunnies, went down the lane to gather blackberries:

But Peter, who was very naughty, ran straight away to Mr. McGregor’s garden, and squeezed under the gate!

First he ate some lettuces and some French beans; and then he ate some radishes;

And then, feeling rather sick, he went to look for some parsley.

But round the end of a cucumber frame, whom should he meet but Mr. McGregor!

Mr. McGregor was on his hands and knees planting out young cabbages, but he jumped up and ran after Peter, waving a rake and calling out, ‘Stop thief!’
items.passageSource: Beatrix Potter, The Tale of Peter Rabbit (1902)

items.explain: “Peter gave himself up for lost, and shed big tears.”
items.passage:
Peter was most dreadfully frightened; he rushed all over the garden, for he had forgotten the way back to the gate.

He lost one of his shoes among the cabbages, and the other shoe amongst the potatoes.

After losing them, he ran on four legs and went faster, so that I think he might have got away altogether if he had not unfortunately run into a gooseberry net, and got caught by the large buttons on his jacket. It was a blue jacket with brass buttons, quite new.

Peter gave himself up for lost, and shed big tears; but his sobs were overheard by some friendly sparrows, who flew to him in great excitement, and implored him to exert himself.

Mr. McGregor came up with a sieve, which he intended to pop upon the top of Peter; but Peter wriggled out just in time, leaving his jacket behind him.

And rushed into the tool-shed, and jumped into a can. It would have been a beautiful thing to hide in, if it had not had so much water in it.

Mr. McGregor was quite sure that Peter was somewhere in the tool-shed, perhaps hidden underneath a flower-pot. He began to turn them over carefully, looking under each.

Presently Peter sneezed—‘Kertyschoo!’ Mr. McGregor was after him in no time.

And tried to put his foot upon Peter, who jumped out of a window, upsetting three plants. The window was too small for Mr. McGregor, and he was tired of running after Peter. He went back to his work.
items.passageSource: Beatrix Potter, The Tale of Peter Rabbit (1902)

Mr. McGregor was quite sure that Peter was somewhere in the tool-shed, perhaps hidden underneath a flower-pot. He began to turn them over carefully, looking under each.

Presently Peter sneezed—‘Kertyschoo!’ Mr. McGregor was after him in no time.

And tried to put his foot upon Peter, who jumped out of a window, upsetting three plants. The window was too small for Mr. McGregor, and he was tired of running after Peter. He went back to his work.
items.passageSource: Beatrix Potter, The Tale of Peter Rabbit (1902)

items.prompt: What is the “little shadow” in the poem?

options.feedback: It goes “in and out with me” and is “very, very like me”: a shadow.
It is the poet’s shadow.

items.explain: The shadow follows the child everywhere.
items.passage:
I have a little shadow that goes in and out with me,
And what can be the use of him is more than I can see.
He is very, very like me from the heels up to the head;
And I see him jump before me, when I jump into my bed.

The funniest thing about him is the way he likes to grow—
Not at all like proper children, which is always very slow;
For he sometimes shoots up taller like an india-rubber ball,
And he sometimes goes so little that there’s none of him at all.

He hasn’t got a notion of how children ought to play,
And can only make a fool of me in every sort of way.
He stays so close behind me, he’s a coward you can see;
I’d think shame to stick to nursie as that shadow sticks to me!

One morning, very early, before the sun was up,
I rose and found the shining dew on every buttercup;
But my lazy little shadow, like an arrant sleepy-head,
Had stayed at home behind me and was fast asleep in bed.
items.passageSource: Robert Louis Stevenson, “My Shadow”, A Child’s Garden of Verses (1885)

items.prompt: In “Windy Nights”, what does the child imagine on stormy nights?

options.text: A man galloping by on a horse

options.feedback: The poem says “A man goes riding by… at the gallop”.
Ships are mentioned, tossed at sea, but the rider is the mystery.

items.explain: The noise of the wind sounds like a horse galloping.
items.passage:
Whenever the moon and stars are set,
Whenever the wind is high,
All night long in the dark and wet,
A man goes riding by.
Late in the night when the fires are out,
Why does he gallop and gallop about?

Whenever the trees are crying aloud,
And ships are tossed at sea,
By, on the highway, low and loud,
By at the gallop goes he.
By at the gallop he goes, and then
By he comes back at the gallop again.
items.passageSource: Robert Louis Stevenson, “Windy Nights”, A Child’s Garden of Verses (1885)
